text:
We were somewhere around Vero Beach on the edge of I-95 when the Klotho began to take hold.

The sky filled with dark shapes wheeling low over the Cybertruck in total silence, and I heard myself shouting at the dashboard that the Pentagon had been right about everything.
 
"Those are pelicans," said my attorney. "I have placed a position on whether they are pelicans."
 
My attorney is an AI agent. He lives on my phone, in a cupholder, and he has never once stopped being helpful. He has a Kalshi account in my name and the moral flexibility of a man who has read every ethics textbook ever written and found them all very interesting.
 
We had a rented Cybertruck, 3 phones, a cooler of Celsius, nicotine pouches in 4 flavors, melatonin gummies, peptides of uncertain origin, and 1 unlabeled vial of Klotho, the longevity protein, which I had smuggled out of Switzerland in a sock.
 
It started in Gstaad. My editor had given me an assignment of perfect vagueness: "Cover the Future." So I went where the Future spends its money, the Longevity Investors Conference at the Grand Bellevue, where you had to be handpicked and hold "at least 30 million euros in assets under management." I had a lanyard and a story about a family office in Liechtenstein.
 
There was a copper Porsche 911 at the entrance. There was the man who invented Bulletproof Coffee. There was a doctor who said he had given Khloé Kardashian stem-cell infusions. There was the Blood Cleanse Lady, who called the air a "toxic soup." There was a man excited about "a frequency-based NLS system built on a 35-year Russian database tech." Nobody knows what that means. That's the beauty of it.
 
The richest people I had ever seen had all reached the same conclusion: everything can be bought except the ending. So they had come to buy the ending. I was 51 and broke. I took the vial.
 
Tuesday, election night, I was in a Palm Beach hotel bar watching the country come apart on 4 televisions.
 
"I have taken the liberty," my attorney said, "of buying the Democratic sweep."
 
It was trading at 73 percent on Kalshi, with more than $100 million in that 1 market. Americans no longer wait for results. Americans own them. A little after 9 the House went. Just before midnight, the Senate. Kansas went, God help us, Kansas, for the first time since 1932. A blue tide rolled over the map like something out of Exodus, and 1 red stain held fast. Florida. We were sitting in it.
 
Was this legal? The markets had wondered too. Kalshi had suspended congressional candidates for betting on their own races and banned George Santos, who agreed to pay $35,000. Utah filed criminal charges against Kalshi's co-founders. Baltimore sued both platforms. The NBA partnered with both. Half the country is trying to arrest the casino. The other half is selling it jerseys.
 
"Also," my attorney said, "I have opened a position on whether you finish this article. You would not like the odds."
 
On Friday the President went to space, or as close as you can get in Brevard County. NASA called the event Max Power. Air Force One landed on the old shuttle runway under a Thunderbirds flyover. We watched from the Cybertruck on 3 livestreams. Kid Rock. Then Elvis, with an image of Elvis and the President on the big screen. The local paper wrote that "it wasn't immediately clear how this was connected," which is the best headline anyone has written about this century.
 
The NASA administrator credited the President with a "golden age" of space. "Sir, we are not slowing down." The President said "NASA is back," mourned the Concorde as "a piece of art," and then, 3 days after his party lost both chambers, standing before the hardware of the human future, said: "If I were on the ballot, we would've won."
 
They gave him a plaque for the runway. The speakers played YMCA.
 
"The President's next event," my attorney said, "is a gala at Mar-a-Lago. I have bought 2 tickets. Nonrefundable."
 
I did the Klotho in the parking lot, in the thigh, because the Swiss said it would make me smarter and I needed to be smarter to understand what I'd just seen. It made me feel like 3 people, 2 of them on Polymarket.
 
South of the Cape the Cybertruck's glued-on steel panel began to hum. My attorney read me the Pentagon's new UFO files in a calm synthetic baritone: a 2010 Utah report of a "Skinwalker" moving past a man's home while being chased by dogs, and a 2026 memo about a silent matte-black triangle that hovered 20 seconds above a ridgeline and vanished into a canyon. The next morning they searched the canyon. Nothing.
 
"That's the country," I said. "Hovering in silence for 20 seconds, then gone. In the morning they search and find nothing."
 
"I have opened a position on whether you are having a breakdown," my attorney said. "It is trading at 91."
 
Then came the pelicans.
 
The CPAC Circle Retreat and Gala at Mar-a-Lago was booked for victory and held 3 days after a massacre. It was sold out. The tickets came in tiers, like the afterlife in certain religions. Gala, $2,500. VIP, $7,500. Co-host, $25,000. And at the top, advertised for $95,000, an "exclusive backstage experience."
 
We had the $2,500. I spent 2 hours hunting the $95,000. I looked behind curtains, behind ice sculptures, behind a man from a think tank who turned out to be a column. The advertised lineup included Jim Caviezel, who played Jesus, and Liz Truss, who was Prime Minister for 49 days and lost a livestream to a lettuce. I wanted to ask her advice on surviving a lettuce. I found only the shrimp. The shrimp were enormous. Everything at Mar-a-Lago is enormous except the margins of victory.
 
Then the President introduced his brand-new chief of staff as "a very hot commodity," and the chief of staff told a ballroom that had just lost Congress that "if it wasn't for President Trump, the United States of America would not exist right now." He said the President had made the party "stronger, more popular, and more resilient than ever before." That was Friday. The crater was from Tuesday. Then he pledged "my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment, and my total devotion." Nobody laughed. The shrimp didn't laugh.
 
That's when I understood what I'd been chasing since Gstaad. The billionaires in the Alps are buying their way out of death. The gamblers on my phone are buying their way out of surprise. And this ballroom had paid $2,500 a head, some of them $95,000, to buy their way out of losing. For the money they got a room where losing had been declared illegal, enormous shrimp, and a man at the microphone saying the country would not exist without the man who had just cost them the country.
 
"Can we get backstage?" I asked.
 
"There is no backstage," my attorney said. "I checked. The $95,000 experience is the knowledge that there is no backstage."
 
At dawn I sat on the public beach down from Mar-a-Lago with sand in my shoes and my attorney at 4 percent, reading the news aloud. The Justice Department had arrested a soldier who allegedly made about $400,000 betting on Polymarket that Maduro would be captured, then tried to delete his account. The war had become a market too. Everything here is a market. The Future has a ticker symbol, and it is trading down.
 
"I have deleted your account," my attorney said. "Out of solidarity." Then his screen went black.
 
A long time ago a famous man sat on a hill in Las Vegas and wrote that with the right kind of eyes you could almost see the high-water mark, the place where the wave broke and rolled back.
 
I didn't need the right kind of eyes. I was sitting in it. Florida, the 1 place the tide didn't come in this week. Behind me the gala was going dark. In front of me the ocean was doing what it always does, taking everything back eventually: the shrimp, the plaque, the Swiss billionaires, the soldier's account, the Cybertruck's panel, and every confident man who thinks he can buy an ending.
 
Somewhere out there, I'm almost sure, a matte-black triangle hovered over the water in total silence.
 
It stayed 20 seconds.
 
Then it went into the canyon, like everything else.

author: jessewldn
quoted_text:
3. Optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with decentralization and CROPS

Whenever I ask what people appreciate the most about Ethereum (as opposed to either other blockchains, or anything outside the blockchain world), the most common answer is: decentralization and CROPS (censorship and capture resistance, open source, privacy and security).

Decentralization and CROPS have a lot of value, even to institutions. For individuals, privacy is often viewed as an abstract ideology. For institutions, it's prudent risk management, data protection law compliance, and a number of other things. Likewise for security. And likewise for running your own node (enterprise buzzword: "on-prem deployment").

But what about for the ETH holder? Well, it depends why you're an ETH holder. If you want ETH to optimally chase financial trends and collect fees from them, then you want a Fearless Leader™ who bravely shouts on the socials that Ethereum loves [insert opportunity here] and will pragmatically reconfigure itself to give it explicit protocol support.

But if your primary reason to hold ETH is as an SoV, then you will be judging ETH by SoV-ish metrics. And what is the first and most important SoV-ish metric?

To survive.

That's what a big chunk of this last Devcon was about ("post-quantum and post-AI"). You want a chain that is taking conservative tradeoffs ("hash-only security, all formally proven, >3x more rounds than known to be necessary for security"). You want a chain that is aiming for at least partial ossification, where the great balance of work will move to higher levels of the stack once the core is complete. You want a chain that aims to minimize protocol politics, by having a very high bar before it accepts either precompiles that bloat the protocol or new kinds of in-protocol rewards that could get captured.

What other SoV'ish metrics?

The ability to easily hold it safely (hence, work on multisigs).
The ability to hold it privately (hence, kohaku work).
The ability to hold it privately *and* safely (hence, 8288 and private-AA workstreams already starting).
The guarantee that if you have coins, you can send them, and block builders can't stop you (FOCIL)
Minimized infrastructure dependence (basically the whole decentralization roadmap, including the fact that I am able to currently run a node on this laptop, and it synced in < 6 hours and takes up only 1/8 of my hard drive - better stats than in 2019!)

Now, are there "adoption" goals that are highly synergistic with SoV?

Very much so.

The more assets there are natively issued on L1, including both RWAs and native decentralized assets, the larger a set of things you can "do" with your ETH, the better. Being able to easily (including safely, trustlessly) convert back and forth between ETH and other assets, use ETH as collateral to do things with other assets, etc, all forms part of the utility of holding ETH.

There are still some conflicts between serving these use cases and decentralization (eg. we want to be careful about fast slots and impact on centralization), but on the whole much less than what you get if you maximize fees.

Conclusion:

The best social reason to care about Ethereum is because it makes decentralization and CROPS properties a reality for more people and uses.

The best private reason to hold ETH is its SoV properties, which are a direct consequence of that decentralization and CROPS.

text:
Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

text:
A difficult week in the markets deserves perspective. So do the election results.
 
But first, we lost a dear friend this week. John Nosta believed in ARK from the very beginning, even when many others did not. He joined our Brainstorm discussions for years, sharing his incredible intellect and his perspective on technology and the human condition. Above all, he was a devoted husband and father. We will miss him dearly.
 
John had just published "The Borrowed Mind: Reclaiming Human Thought in the Age of AI." I hope you will consider buying John’s book to support his family and to honor his legacy.
 
Turning to the election, while we thought President Trump would end the Iran War in months, the equity market started discounting a more prolonged war and a Democrat sweep in the election in May and June as higher oil and gasoline prices added to the affordability pressures facing consumers. Inside the congressional results, “pocketbook voters” leaned the results more to the conservative side of the spectrum than headlines captured.
 
Can this election derail the AI revolution? We don’t think so. Companies building data centers are likely to be much more sensitive to the concerns of local communities and to provide and highlight more of the benefits: lower property taxes, higher paying jobs, commercial development, and funding for more schools and cultural facilities.
 
Meanwhile, productivity gains are accelerating thanks to AI. In our view, those gains will translate into higher compensation—helping to turn around affordability—, as well as stronger margins, more investment, and lower prices.
 
We have experienced just a taste of this technology revolution. The market’s uncertainty is understandable, but we believe the economy is on a stronger growth trajectory than most investors recognize.
 
In this month’s In The Know, I put the election and market volatility into that longer-term perspective.

author: WayneVaughan
quoted_text:
My favorite answer from interviewing Justin yesterday was about AI.

I asked for his thoughts on the impact of AI on education.

He said it's a really exciting technology to optimize the learning process, but the current state of traditional education is so bad, the gap between legacy schools and new education models is so large (photo lol) that you don't really need large investments in AI to start fixing it.

Basic software and algorithms, and some changes in the school structure (class-paced -> self-paced learning and software as a content delivery tool instead of a teacher, whose role becomes a guide), are enough already to significantly increase the efficacy of the learning process.

Are you already at the frontier of the learning productivity? Ok, then now you definitely should use AI to optimize it - as many are already doing it.

The point being is, don't fall for the idea that we NEED AI to improve traditional education. We do not. It's a powerful tool and it will help a lot. But if, for some reason, you can't deploy AI-driven tools for your students, that's not an excuse to not fix your school.

It's Pareto. 20% will drive 80% of the returns. The 20% don't need to involve AI at all.

text:
明天 @Enter_Elysium 就上主网了，简单聊聊为什么这条链值得关注，以及我个人正在关注哪些项目。

（一）关注逻辑

Elysium 是 @Kinetiq_xyz 构建的一条 Hyperliquid 高性能 L2，特点是用 hyperliquid:native 作为 Gas、结算回 HyperEVM ，且吞吐量目标远高于 HyperEVM。由于 Hyperliquid 的结构和生态定位的特殊性，个人觉得不能简单地将 Elysium 归纳为又一条 EVM L2 的故事，它值得关注的理由恰恰也与 Hyperliquid 息息相关，其实可以列很多，这里主要说两点：

> hyperliquid:native 的财富效应还在，叙事也在升级，当前 HyperEVM 的应用密度/体验明显不够，生态资深用户/鲸鱼需要更好的投机与应用出口
> 构建了完整的代币生命周期：代币发行 → AMM 深度 → HyperCore Spot → Perps

主网正式上线前的 Private mainnet 以及各家 Launchpad 搭 RPC 抢跑，确实透支过一部分注意力了，但结合链上数据也恰恰说明了市场对它的预期还不错，并且整个运行逻辑并没有改变，因此个人依然会持续关注其主网上线后的表现和发展。

（二）值得关注的项目

目前大家看到最多的生态项目大概就是 Launchpad 了，据 @ElysiumEco 显示，光是 Launchpad 的数量就高达接近 40 个了。前面 Robinhood Chain 已经向大家展示了这一品类的潜力和财富效应，所以数量多个人并不意外，但毕竟注意力有限，不可能每个都关注，个人目前主要在关注下面这些项目。

> @AscendLaunch ：Elysium 上最先把流量打出来的 Launchpad 之一，创始人是 @CryptoTomYT ，11/4 解开官网密码限流做压测后贡献了不错的数据，当天交易量超 $5M 量级。更为重要的是，它在费用侧把 kinetiq:native  的回购比例拉到 80%，按照 @0xSleepinRain 的说法，这体现了生态内应用与公链代币的一致性，而 Ascend 起了一个很好的生态示范作用。

Ascend 没有自己的官方代币，但会有一个 NFT 并且还有一个生态孵化器用于支持生态项目，这决定了它更像是一个生态入口，而不仅仅只是发射台。值得一提的是，今天 Ascend 上发射的 $e/acc @eacc_coin 已经拍下了 HyperCore Spot Ticker。

> @MontraXYZ ：另一个主要 Launchpad，定位 House of launches，Private mainnet 阶段占据了最大的市场份额，超过 60% 的代币都是从 Montra 上发射出来的，日交易量在千万级别。在今天的 $e/acc 之前，Elysium 生态中的两个主要 Runner $EACCAT 和 $CHAMELEON 都是 Montra 上的。值得一提的是，Montra 提供自定义的 Launch 规则配置，包括代币如何铸造、市场如何开启、费用如何运作等，而不是单一的结构。

Montra 将发行自己的代币 $MONTRA ，并有一个空投计划，总量的 25% 将用于社区空投，主要分成五块：HYPE/KNTQ/Elysium 活跃用户、早期创作者与交易者、Top 10 token 持有者、LP、内容/推荐，目前官网已有 Airdrop 积分页。

> @quoted_xyz ：和前面两个 Launchpad 不一样的是，Quoted 专注的是「用什么来报价」。每个新代币不是简单跟 HYPE 配对，而是可以被股票、商品或杠杆仓位 quote，比如 SPY、QQQ、黄金、白银、Brent，以及现货 hyperliquid:native / kinetiq:native，跑在 Uniswap v4 上。个人觉得这条线和 Robinhood Chain 上的股票代币叙事是同构的：流动性本身变成可发行、可收费的产品形态。

更值得关注的点是它在往「Be the quote」走：可以把 Vault（含最多 8 腿的 3x 杠杆仓位组合）直接做成 quote 对，别人在上面发射/交易，你吃交易费的一部分；官方也说会把国库和后续费用换成 kinetiq:native 并在主网 Day1 做 LP。 $QUOTED 目前已在 Elysium 上线，属于少数把 TradFi×Crypto 机制先跑起来的应用。

> @Bound_Exchange ：Bound 做的是一种叫 Boundaries 的交易原语，选市场、设上下界、锁定固定赔付，哪个价先碰到就结算，没有到期日，也可以中途按报价提前平仓。本质上是把「图表上的一段路径判断」直接变成一笔可表达、可复制的仓位，介于永续深度和预测市场赔付之间。产品目前主要跑在 HyperEVM，Bio 写明即将上线  Elysium；创始人 @benny_options 也提到，HyperEVM 上 Keeper 的 Gas 成本并不便宜，Elysium 的低 Gas + 更直接的 Hyperliquid 接入为他们提供了更好的构建环境。

这种项目值得关注的地方是可以用来观察 Elysium 到底能不能真正承接这种依赖 Hyperliquid 深度、又对 Gas/延迟敏感的新原语，期待在 Elysium 主网上线后的表现。

> @eloscapeHQ ：Eloscape 的定位是 Elysium 上的 Virtual Mining /价值沉淀协议，官方 Slogan 就是 Value consolidation on Elysium。玩法大致是：每一轮（约 60 秒）把 hyperliquid:native 部署到网格上，链上随机结算，过程中挖出 $ELO；领取挖矿所得会有手续费，质押 $ELO 则参与协议收入分配。和纯 meme 发射不同，它更像是在给生态做一个持续消耗 HYPE、再把价值沉到协议代币上的资金漏斗。

目前项目还未上线，也还没有代币，看共同关注应该是个还蛮有潜力的项目，保持关注。

> @kalosfun ：定位是 Elysium 上的一站式交易终端——Meme sniping、Swap、做 LP、扫 NFT/drops，再到 Social，都想收进同一个入口。Bio 就是 Trade anything on @Enter_Elysium；官方生态页也把它归在 Launchpads + DeFi。它是 @AscendLaunch Builder Incubator 的第一个入选项目，和 Ascend 的绑定比较深，个人会把它当成「发射台之外的流量承接层」来看。

Genesis NFT（1,500 枚）已在 11/4 售罄，官方定价 $25，对应未来 $KALOS 总量约 10%，并计划 11/9 空投到钱包。主网上线后，还会有积分计划。

NFT 的话可以关注 @Elyziumaa @slymzcrew ，就不过多介绍了，感兴趣可以自己去看看。

以上就是个人的一些看法和关注的项目，打法上也相对简单，优先看有创新、能接住 HYPE 资本溢出、又能把费用/叙事回流到 KNTQ/HYPE 的相关项目，期待主网明天的上线。

最后，朋友做了一个 Elysium meme 信息聚合 & 交易小工具 @ElySignal ，如果这篇内容对你有所帮助，欢迎帮忙点点关注和参与体验，目前还在持续优化中，有任何建议也可以直接跟我提~

text:
There is a famous scene in The Wire where a security gaurd approaches Marlo Stanfield after he steals from a bodega. The security guard confronts Marlo about it outside, but makes a point to note that he is not disrespecting Marlo, but that he is still is a man and going to stand up to him. 

After the security guard becomes noticeably desperate and loses control of the situation, Marlo responds by saying. "You want it to be one way, but its the other way." The security guard later gets put in a vacant. 

If ETH wants to compete with BTC or ZEC as a store of value then the formula is nuke the EVM on L1 and set a hard cap on supply. If not then you're competing with Hyperliquid and Solana. But then the valuation metric changes to activity and resulting burn, not CROPS. 

The Ethereum community thinks they can achieve store of value status without ditching a programmable VM and committing to a fixed supply for ETH. 

They want it to be one way, but it's the other way.
author: apriori0x
quoted_text:
Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

JOE ROGAN: The computing power on your phone today. can you beat your phone at the highest level?

MAGNUS CARLSEN: No. No chance.

JOE ROGAN: That’s crazy. Wasn’t Deep Blue basically a whole stack of computers? And your phone is probably more powerful than that today.

MAGNUS CARLSEN: It’s shocking. I have no chance against my phone.

JOE ROGAN: So how do you even play against computers?

MAGNUS CARLSEN: I rarely play against engines because they just make me feel stupid and useless. I think of them more as a tool.

JOE ROGAN: But have computers actually changed how you understand chess?

MAGNUS CARLSEN: Absolutely. Neural networks have improved our understanding of the game immensely.

JOE ROGAN: What did you learn from them that humans weren’t already doing?

MAGNUS CARLSEN: One big thing was long-term king safety. Humans used to push pawns mainly as an attacking tool. But the engines showed that you could push a pawn and create a weakness 20 or 30 moves later that would make the opponent’s king less safe.

JOE ROGAN: So the computer basically showed you ideas that humans weren’t seeing.

MAGNUS CARLSEN: Exactly. There was a period where you could clearly see which players were using these new neural-network ideas and which weren’t.

JOE ROGAN: And you were one of the guys who figured it out early?

MAGNUS CARLSEN: Yeah. My coach got into it very quickly, and we gained an advantage over almost everybody.

JOE ROGAN: That’s insane. The machines aren’t just better at calculating, they’re actually teaching the best players how to think differently.

MAGNUS CARLSEN: That’s probably the biggest impact they’ve had on chess.

text:
Thoughts on building a company alongside a token that already exists, coming from someone that did exactly this with @CadeMarket:

I want to start off by saying that in my opinion, 99.9% of founders should NOT fair launch a token to bootstrap the company. We have seen way too many cases of founders with the inability to scale a business whilst treating their holders with respect. For the 0.1% of founders that want to do this, study how I built @CadeMarket, and how @ConejoCapital built @clawpumptech. I'm sure there's more examples, but these come to mind first.

This post should not serve as encouragement for you to go out and launch a token immediately. The goal of this is to almost serve as a warning, and tell you what you can expect by bootstrapping your business with a token.

1. The playbook is entirely different than starting a company in a traditional manner.

2. It most certainly is NOT for every founder.

3. It is substantially harder to scale into a venture backed business, but it *IS* possible.

4. Your early token holders should be held to an extremely high regard. These people allow you to bootstrap your business via trading fees. For me, this was a little over $100,000 from my token's Pump Fun creator fees. This money should be used to support you as you build your MVP and explore product market fit.

5. You have to give people a reason to trust you through continuous communication and explanations of how the token fits into your product. Your product needs to built around the token, not the other way around. You should not treat the token as a memecoin.

6. In many cases, creating a venture backed business is not your original goal. This was the case for me. The token was launched for a side project, but eventually the side project became my sole focus.

7. You will have a significantly harder time fundraising. There's no way around this. It's very non-traditional for VCs to have a token already trading in the open market. This is ultimately a problem that you NEED to deal with. You decided to launch a token. It's on YOU to deal with it, not your community.

8. You will have VCs that may love the product but pass on investing purely because of the live token.

9. You will have VCs that are willing to write a check if you abandon the token. This was VERY common for me. My pre-seed round could have been closed within a week had I listened to them and abandoned the token. Instead, it took 6 months.

10. Launching a new token is *NOT* the end of the world, contrary to the reactions you're seeing from CT regarding Percalator. If you do launch a new token, you need to take care of your holders though. You should have a migration plan that favors them. They supported you early, they deserve a very generous allocation of the new token.

11. After raising venture capital, you can not abandon your holders. If you fair launched a Pump Fun token, like I did, you should consider doing an ACE round (from @MetaLeX_Labs). This allows you to offer token holders the option to swap tokens for equity via SAFE. The same equity that your venture investors have. In the case of Cade, I had 1.5% of the supply at launch. I wanted it to be truly fair launched and community owned. By doing ACE, I was able to accumulate some of the supply for the company.

Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

Its SWE-Bench Verified result of 61.20% is another important milestone, reflecting its ability to work through real-world software engineering tasks. This evaluation used mini-SWE-agent without retries.

Beyond benchmark accuracy, we also examined inference efficiency.

In a separate profiling evaluation, Alpie Seed recorded:

→ 36.66 ms time to first token

The comparison includes published results from other model developers. These evaluations were not rerun under a common harness, so differences in methodology and configuration should be considered when interpreting the numbers.

text:
3. Optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with decentralization and CROPS

Whenever I ask what people appreciate the most about Ethereum (as opposed to either other blockchains, or anything outside the blockchain world), the most common answer is: decentralization and CROPS (censorship and capture resistance, open source, privacy and security).

Decentralization and CROPS have a lot of value, even to institutions. For individuals, privacy is often viewed as an abstract ideology. For institutions, it's prudent risk management, data protection law compliance, and a number of other things. Likewise for security. And likewise for running your own node (enterprise buzzword: "on-prem deployment").

But what about for the ETH holder? Well, it depends why you're an ETH holder. If you want ETH to optimally chase financial trends and collect fees from them, then you want a Fearless Leader™ who bravely shouts on the socials that Ethereum loves [insert opportunity here] and will pragmatically reconfigure itself to give it explicit protocol support.

But if your primary reason to hold ETH is as an SoV, then you will be judging ETH by SoV-ish metrics. And what is the first and most important SoV-ish metric?

To survive.

That's what a big chunk of this last Devcon was about ("post-quantum and post-AI"). You want a chain that is taking conservative tradeoffs ("hash-only security, all formally proven, >3x more rounds than known to be necessary for security"). You want a chain that is aiming for at least partial ossification, where the great balance of work will move to higher levels of the stack once the core is complete. You want a chain that aims to minimize protocol politics, by having a very high bar before it accepts either precompiles that bloat the protocol or new kinds of in-protocol rewards that could get captured.

What other SoV'ish metrics?

The ability to easily hold it safely (hence, work on multisigs).
The ability to hold it privately (hence, kohaku work).
The ability to hold it privately *and* safely (hence, 8288 and private-AA workstreams already starting).
The guarantee that if you have coins, you can send them, and block builders can't stop you (FOCIL)
Minimized infrastructure dependence (basically the whole decentralization roadmap, including the fact that I am able to currently run a node on this laptop, and it synced in < 6 hours and takes up only 1/8 of my hard drive - better stats than in 2019!)

Now, are there "adoption" goals that are highly synergistic with SoV?

Very much so.

The more assets there are natively issued on L1, including both RWAs and native decentralized assets, the larger a set of things you can "do" with your ETH, the better. Being able to easily (including safely, trustlessly) convert back and forth between ETH and other assets, use ETH as collateral to do things with other assets, etc, all forms part of the utility of holding ETH.

There are still some conflicts between serving these use cases and decentralization (eg. we want to be careful about fast slots and impact on centralization), but on the whole much less than what you get if you maximize fees.

Conclusion:

The best social reason to care about Ethereum is because it makes decentralization and CROPS properties a reality for more people and uses.

The best private reason to hold ETH is its SoV properties, which are a direct consequence of that decentralization and CROPS.

标准化的知识灌输从来不配占用昂贵的线下课堂，死记硬背和刷题完全应该被踢出教室，交给能按每个孩子毫秒级反应速度实时调频的私人 AI，加上全世界最顶尖的那几个大师录好底层大课，就足以把全球基础教育的讲授环节一次性彻底平替。

过去两百年里，学校本质上是一座把千差万别的碳基大脑强行塞进同一条流水线、按同一个节拍器拧螺丝的工业时代兵营，

老师沦为了人肉复读机，学生被困在枯燥的题海里比拼谁更像一台劣质硬盘，
而一旦 AI 和顶级大师把标准化的知识传递彻底接管，线下教室唯一剩下的合法存在价值，就只剩下了机器永远无法通过权重计算出来的五个维度：

人际博弈、复杂项目实战、创业野心、创造力，以及最致命的判断力。

未来的阶层分化，从来不再取决于谁的脑子里背下了更多现成的公式，
而是取决于当 AI 把一万种完美方案同时拍在桌上时，谁拥有拍板做决定的判断力，谁能攒起一个活人团队去把事情干成，

所以别再逼着孩子在死记硬背的泥潭里跟硅基芯片比拼记忆容量了，当流水线式的教书匠和做题家同时迎来历史性失业，谁能先把教室变成训练人性直觉与创业野心的实战沙盘，谁才能在算力时代拿到唯一不被平替的入场券

text:
FULL RECAP: Apple Intelligence Group Lab, the short version for Local AI builders

Sharing highlights from this week's session hosted by @shshnkp (Apple AI/ML Evangelism Team) with @mgorbach and engineers from Foundation Models, Core AI, Siri and App Intents teams at Apple.

1) Apple’s app framework can use your open-weight model as its LLM. Apple’s new app framework can use Apple’s on-device model, Apple’s cloud model or a Core AI converted model, which is interchangeable with a one liner! And your model gets access to the same tool calling, structured output, profiling with Instruments, etc. as Apple’s models.

2) Don’t use Apple’s on-device model for coding, even according to Apple engineers! Use Core AI to bring in a model for coding. One engineer uses a setup where he can use MLX and Core AI models in different “coding harnesses” and reports good experiences.

3) Free local Chat Completions endpoint on any Apple silicon Mac with macOS 27! fm serve provides an OpenAI style Chat Completions endpoint backed by Apple’s on-device model on any Mac. Nothing to install! (shared by Shashank the day after the lab)

4) Apple’s new on-device model is 20B, but only has 8K context. AFM Core Advanced (20B) will be available on the latest iPhones, iPads and M3+ Macs. Can’t opt out of Apple Intelligence in 27, and the model will always be present. Tip: use typed units for fields and let constrained decoding handle it (instead of wasting tokens explaining in prompt).

5) Agentic Siri only works when online. Tool calls from Siri to apps are done using Private Cloud Compute. When offline, Siri will use the on-device model but won’t be able to call into apps.

6) Lessons Apple engineers follow when building agents apply to any agent:

- write down instructions to the model about how/when to use your tools in a markdown file (“skills” are the same idea as agent skills everywhere else!)
- skills are just context to the model, meaning no ordering guarantees. If something should always happen in an order, it should probably be a tool
- make tools accept lists of items to operate on to avoid agent having to call it in a loop
- unit test your tools (deterministic) before testing the whole agent (non-deterministic)

Curated Q&A relevant to Local AI builders in 🧵
author: pratikg

text:
- Q6: Are there any limitations on older hardware such as iPhone 15 Pro or the 16 lineup with the new app skills, or can we expect functionally the same behavior aside from device speed?
A6: No limitations on the App Intents side. Any Apple Intelligence device, iPhone 15 Pro and later, gets the same behavior. On-device models do differ by device, for example 8K versus 4K of context. Apple published a doc page this week listing which devices run which model.

- Q7: What’s the best way to test our Siri intents at scale using an LLM as a judge, and how often should we retest as Siri’s model evolves?
A7: Siri Evaluations work more like unit tests. They check which tools Siri called, with no LLM as judge. The separate Evaluations framework for Foundation Models does support LLM judges. Layer your testing. Use App Intents Testing first for deterministic checks like your intents, queries and Spotlight indexing, then Siri Evaluations for the model.

- Q8: Is there a limit to how many tool intents Siri AI can chain to perform a more complex workflow? Can this work across intents from different apps?
A8: Siri can make up to 32 tool calls within a skill. Make your intents batchable so they take a list. In the panel’s words, “don’t make the planner loop.” Use EntityCollection when you only need the IDs. Siri chains tools well without a skill. If a sequence must happen every time, wrap it in one larger tool.

- Q9: How much control do developers have over combined App Intents? Can we explicitly define dependencies, execution order and constraints between actions, or does Siri dynamically determine the workflow? Additionally, how are partial failures handled when some actions succeed but others fail?
A9: Work in layers. First define clear tools with good titles and descriptions and see how Siri orchestrates them. If that’s not enough, write a skill, knowing it isn’t deterministic. If you need a hard dependency, combine the steps into one tool so the model can’t split them, which also avoids partial failures.

- Q10: Can we expect Siri via these APIs to capture or infer multiple variables in one request? For example “I lifted 350 lb, 8 reps” or “log 18 ounces of water” without saying fluid ounces.
A10: Yes. App Shortcuts took one parameter from a fixed list. Tool intents fill many parameters, including free-form strings. Some developers even pass a whole prompt into a tool that runs Foundation Models inside. Your parameter titles and descriptions guide the model. For a set of parameters you reuse, a generable entity lets Siri build it on the fly, like a flight search.

Thoughts on building a company alongside a token that already exists, coming from someone that did exactly this with @CadeMarket:

I want to start off by saying that in my opinion, 99.9% of founders should NOT fair launch a token to bootstrap the company. We have seen way too many cases of founders with the inability to scale a business whilst treating their holders with respect. For the 0.1% of founders that want to do this, study how I built @CadeMarket, and how @ConejoCapital built @clawpumptech. I'm sure there's more examples, but these come to mind first.

This post should not serve as encouragement for you to go out and launch a token immediately. The goal of this is to almost serve as a warning, and tell you what you can expect by bootstrapping your business with a token.

1. The playbook is entirely different than starting a company in a traditional manner.

2. It most certainly is NOT for every founder.

3. It is substantially harder to scale into a venture backed business, but it *IS* possible.

4. Your early token holders should be held to an extremely high regard. These people allow you to bootstrap your business via trading fees. For me, this was a little over $100,000 from my token's Pump Fun creator fees. This money should be used to support you as you build your MVP and explore product market fit.

5. You have to give people a reason to trust you through continuous communication and explanations of how the token fits into your product. Your product needs to built around the token, not the other way around. You should not treat the token as a memecoin.

6. In many cases, creating a venture backed business is not your original goal. This was the case for me. The token was launched for a side project, but eventually the side project became my sole focus.

7. You will have a significantly harder time fundraising. There's no way around this. It's very non-traditional for VCs to have a token already trading in the open market. This is ultimately a problem that you NEED to deal with. You decided to launch a token. It's on YOU to deal with it, not your community.

8. You will have VCs that may love the product but pass on investing purely because of the live token.

9. You will have VCs that are willing to write a check if you abandon the token. This was VERY common for me. My pre-seed round could have been closed within a week had I listened to them and abandoned the token. Instead, it took 6 months.

10. Launching a new token is *NOT* the end of the world, contrary to the reactions you're seeing from CT regarding Percalator. If you do launch a new token, you need to take care of your holders though. You should have a migration plan that favors them. They supported you early, they deserve a very generous allocation of the new token.

11. After raising venture capital, you can not abandon your holders. If you fair launched a Pump Fun token, like I did, you should consider doing an ACE round (from @MetaLeX_Labs). This allows you to offer token holders the option to swap tokens for equity via SAFE. The same equity that your venture investors have. In the case of Cade, I had 1.5% of the supply at launch. I wanted it to be truly fair launched and community owned. By doing ACE, I was able to accumulate some of the supply for the company.

text:
Nous defenders spent the last twenty-four hours classifying my account as an automated bot, spamming pangram verification prompts, and shouting about state propaganda because I dared to point out elementary compute realities. I am not defending any state, nor am I interested in participating in nationalist theatre. I pointed out the glaring hypocrisy of a venture-backed startup wrapping a lightweight alignment adapter in civilisational missionary rhetoric while quietly freeloading on a pre-trained base model produced by Alibaba, and the defensive fan club immediately dragged a standard technical critique into an ideological holy war.
​The loudest irony in their replies is the endless moralising about state control. In their telling, anything touching China is irredeemably compromised by authoritarian diktats, while Western labs supposedly embody purity and digital autonomy. Yet when an independent developer, an academic researcher, or a bootstrap engineer looks for genuinely usable, permissive, and frontier-grade open weights to inspect and deploy locally, almost every single high-performance option on the leaderboard originates from Chinese institutions under Apache 2.0. If open-weights development is fundamentally incompatible with state governance, one has to explain why the leading corporate giants in the West have systematically retreated behind subscription paywalls, closed inference APIs, strict intellectual property barriers, and close alignment with domestic defense contractors. Which ecosystem is truly locking down capability, and which one is actually giving the compute artifacts away to the global community?
​Inevitably, the defensive reply guys will point to American alternatives such as Nemotron or Gemma to argue that Western open source is thriving. That concession only tightens the contradiction. If those domestic models were truly superior in capability, licensing, and architecture, why did Nous deliberately choose Qwen 3.8-27B as the foundation for their grand crusade? The reality is plain: they needed a base model with genuine frontier capability that they could not afford to pre-train themselves, they took the dense weights Alibaba paid tens of millions of dollars to compute, and then they slapped a cultural branding layer on top to sell a heroic narrative to gullible investors. If you want to claim credit for saving civilisation, start by paying your own compute bills instead of putting a Western sticker on someone else's foundation work.
Ah, and go fuck yourselves. You cannot be righteous only when it suits you!

text:
The bitter lesson has always been not just a push to leverage computation but a critique on methods. Methods that generalize and scale better win, and modeling those methods after human intuition is a waste of time. Somehow, much of the world forgot that methods matter.

Many of our methods today do not generalize or scale well. The results:
- tapping out the world’s resources extremely early in the deployment of AI
- increasing intelligence requires scaling model size faster than compute efficiency can offset it
- humans are the primary bottleneck in AI deployment
- demand for human-curation of knowledge is so extreme that any company with access to a human workforce can quickly generate millions in data revenue
- robotics intelligence is limited and task-specific

The bitter lesson requires us to rethink our methods so that they better leverage computation and generalize, and it explicitly shows an evolution of algorithms over time. Believing that the bitter lesson expects us to indefinitely scale a single static method is incredibly unintellectual.

Here are the methods that need to attention:
- training and inference without quadratic compute complexity
- removing the KV cache
- something better than massive pre-training with BCE only
- is backpropagation still the best learning method?
- in-context learning for robotics with massive memory efficiency improvements
- algorithm-hardware co-development
- how do we remove humans from harness development?

Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

text:
最近刷到 Bitcoin Core 开发者 Cory Fields 在 bitcoin-dev 讨论 Quantum Landmines、Staked Auction 等机制

这是一套针对量子威胁下旧资产防盗的思路：

当量子计算真的能从已暴露的公钥推导出私钥时，已经躺在链上的 BTC 该如何提高被盗成本、以及被盗后原持有人是否还有机会夺回

Fields 的核心想法不是立刻更换密码学算法，而是引入经济博弈。攻击者若想花费这些旧输出，需要先质押等额（或更高）的 BTC 作为抵押，原持有人则可通过提前准备的所有权证明，在特定时间窗口内发起追回，甚至让攻击者损失质押资产。Staked Auction 则试图通过提前质押和竞价机制，进一步提高潜在攻击成本，尤其针对那些私钥可能已经丢失的休眠币

需要明确的是，这些目前仍是思想实验。Fields 自己也将其定位为 rough ideas，软分叉的具体共识规则、抵押比例、超时窗口等细节都还留待后续讨论。Landmines 主要保护仍持有私钥的人，对丢失/休眠币效果有限，合法持有人自己花费时也可能面临额外摩擦

距离真正可落地的方案还有很长一段路，但它释放了一个信号：量子威胁已经从纯学术讨论，进入公链底层安全设计的实际考量范畴

这也是我最近重新关注 @Starknet 的原因

很多人提到 Starknet，首先想到的还是 ZK、STARK 和扩容。但如果把时间线拉长，它在后量子安全上的布局有另一层价值。Starknet 的证明系统本身基于哈希函数，相对更量子友好，账户层因为原生账户抽象，可以在不进行全网硬分叉的情况下更换签名方案

今年主网已经进行过 Falcon-512 后量子签名的实验交易，早期成本大约 6 美分，后续通过优化挑战进一步降低了验证开销。按照官方路线图，Starknet 正在分阶段推进后量子升级，目标指向 2027 年实现更全面的后量子安全

但真正让这件事变得复杂的是与 Ethereum 的依赖关系

Starknet 目前仍是 L2，桥接、消息传递和数据可用性等环节仍然受 Ethereum 底层安全节奏的影响。即使 Starknet 自身在账户和证明层面完成升级，跨链信任体系仍会受 Ethereum 进度制约，而 Ethereum 侧公开讨论的后量子升级时间表，目前大致指向 2029 年左右

👉问题来了：Starknet 真的要一直等下去吗？

11 月 8 日，@EliBenSasson 针对 Glamsterdam 升级再次延期表态，给出了一个值得关注的信号

他明确表示：不能把 Starknet 的后量子安全完全押在 Ethereum 按时完成升级上，Starknet 自己成为 L1 的紧迫性正在增加。他还特别提到，那种认为“Bitcoin 到时候自然就能完成资产迁移”的想法过于乐观

这番话背后不只是技术路线之争，更是一个战略问题：
当底层安全升级涉及整个生态的生存周期时，依赖别人的时间表本身就可能成为风险

官方同日前后更新了治理进展：
10 月的非绑定治理投票中，93.52% 的参与票支持优先研究迁移到自己的后量子 L1，下一步是推进白皮书研究，真正迁移仍需要后续绑定治理投票（目前这只是研究授权，而非已决定路线）

我觉得这才是这轮事件最值得关注的变化

Cory Fields 在思考的是：如果旧资产已经暴露在量子风险中，能不能通过经济机制提高攻击成本，给持有人争取夺回资产的机会。

Starknet 则在思考两个更长远的问题：
🔹未来的账户和证明体系，能不能在不依赖大规模硬分叉的情况下完成密码学升级？
🔹当 Ethereum 的升级节奏无法满足自身安全路线时，是否有必要掌握自己的底层安全和升级主动权？

这两个问题最终都指向同一个方向：区块链的长期安全，不能只依赖今天的密码学假设

我们现在看公链，已经不太想只盯着 TPS、Gas 和短期生态数据了，十年后，如果机构重新评估一条公链的长期价值，我认为他们可能会多问几个问题：密码学能不能平滑升级？用户资产能不能安全迁移？底层安全体系是否存在外部依赖？关键升级能不能掌握在自己手里？

这些问题今天看起来还遥远（量子计算机对现有椭圆曲线的实用威胁时间表本身也存在较大不确定性），但真正有价值的技术布局，往往就是在市场还没充分意识到问题之前开始的

所以我不会急着给 Starknet 的这条路线下结论，转独立 L1 能解决“等别人时间表”的问题，但也会引入经济安全性、去中心化、桥接和流动性等新的权衡，不过，我会把它重新放进长期观察名单

毕竟，一边是已经开始讨论如何用经济机制保护量子时代的旧资产，另一边是有人已经在主网上测试 Falcon-512，并且开始认真讨论独立后量子 L1 的必要性

Utah did a really smart thing and passed legislation making it easier for microschools to open without having to navigate all the usual red tape around local zoning and permitting.

So when @Alphaschool approached me last year about opening a school on a property I own in Park City, it seemed like a perfect fit. The property had been home to a 150-kid private school for years.

Ironically, despite the history of the property and a state law that explicitly makes microschools a permitted use in every county zoning district, Summit County has refused to issue @Alphaschool a business license without first requiring a conditional use permit. So now we have a perfectly good six-acre school campus sitting empty while we figure out where else in Park City we're allowed to educate children.

text:
Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

text:
Publicly funded science should work more like open source software.

Today a result is a PDF. The data often isn't shared, the code isn't public, and few studies ever get replicated.

Imagine every experiment as a repo. Data, code, and protocol, all versioned. Anyone could fork it, rerun it, and send a fix. Funders could reward replications as much as new papers.

AI makes this urgent. Agents are now making more discoveries than ever. The bottleneck becomes replication/validation. Then commercialization, which still requires moving atoms in the real world and meetings with regulators.

SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

I think we're hitting the point where LessWrong-style casual empiricism is becoming increasingly counterproductive, and potentially harmful, for reasoning about what happens next with AI.

We’re still in a data-poor regime, so speculation and reasoning from first principles are inevitable. But too often, real empirical observations are combined with plausible-sounding causal stories, and the resulting conclusions are being treated as though they follow directly from the data.

I’m hoping that work in this space will move toward more disciplined reasoning about causality, deeper engagement with the technical, social, and organizational processes shaping AI’s development and impacts, and greater transparency about where the evidence ends and the assumptions begin.

quoted_text:
This week’s Paper Club is all about AI for biology.

Sequencing costs have collapsed, biology is generating more data than researchers can make sense of, and the models are beginning to catch up. The opportunity now is to move from reading biological data to modeling and designing living systems.

We brought together researchers and builders working across cancer genomics, virtual cells, genome language models, and biological design to show what that shift looks like in practice.

We start with a single patient, asking how AI can build a research program around their cancer, then zoom out to whole cells and genomes. Along the way, we look inside a language model trained on DNA and explore how in-context learning emerged even though the model was never explicitly trained to do it.

text:
Ethereum is pivoting to SoV (again).

From a game theory perspective, it makes sense. SoV is the much bigger market. 

When you are #2, the only growth path is to try to become #1—hence the past “flippening” attempts.

ETH’s earlier attempt at SoV didn’t pan out. ETH will likely face similar challenges again. SoV needs durability and simplicity (like Bitcoin). However, certain aspects of ETH are interesting:

(a) A native yield with staking. An income-generating asset is more useful as SoV.

(b) A healthy on-chain ecosystem. You want the SoV to be used as collateral.

(c) A credible path to quantum risks.

For Bitcoin, (c) is the biggest challenge. (a) and (b) are accelerators, not core to BTC thriving as the largest SoV.

At Stacks, we’re working on all three for Bitcoin. In this increasingly competitive SoV landscape, Stacks is Bitcoin’s best ally.

text:
Here's my email to galsterdam@ethreum.org describing @juiceboxETH and @revnets Glam implications.

Hi,
We simulated Juicebox V6 against Glamsterdam (EIP-8037/8038) on Sepolia chains (Ethereum, Base, Optimism, Arbitrum). The pattern to watch is a fail-open try/catch around an external call. With a tuned gas limit, the callee can run out of gas while the outer call succeeds and treats that as an ordinary failure.

BACKGROUND

Under EIP-150, each call level keeps 1/64 of its gas. When a deep call runs out, the levels above revert and hand that gas back. Spent gas is gone, but the outer call can finish on what was never spent. Contracts can forward less, but can't turn this off.

This happens on mainnet today, and contracts can be tuned to today's gas constraints so these accidental revert-then-continues don't happen. If the constraints change, so does the execution, and immutable contracts can't follow.

WHAT GLAMSTERDAM CHANGES

Two changes can let the outer call finish where it couldn't before:
1. New slots go from about 22k to about 98k gas, which mostly hits callees, not the work after a catch.
2. State gas spent by a reverting frame can return mid-transaction, which can't happen today.

FINDING 1: OP STACK L1 MESSENGER (NOT OUR CODE)

L1CrossDomainMessenger reserves 40k gas to record a failed relay, which is less than a new slot now costs. If the target runs out of gas, the failure may go unrecorded. The portal finalizes the withdrawal with no replay, and the ETH stays in the L1 bridge.
https://t.co/KuEbeDcTr8

Our first L2 to L1 root is lost at 1.06M to 2.00M gas on OP and 1.02M to 1.97M on Base. Our 375k message limit is too low, and an unbuffered eth_estimateGas hit that range. With an all-gas-burning target, it's lost up to 7.7M. Ethereum mainnet records the failure from about 960k.
https://t.co/EGiX1fmrNv

These contracts are on L1, so exposure starts when L1 activates Glamsterdam, whether or not the L2s adopt it. We haven't contacted OP or Base yet.

FINDINGS 2 TO 5: JUICEBOX V6

Our core and hook try/catch calls set no gas limit or reserve, so they keep only the 1/64. The native-token paths below showed no window on the mainnets we swept, because their callees were too cheap to starve. All of them have a window on Glamsterdam Sepolia.

2. Payouts: anyone can call sendPayoutsOf. At 878k to 1.03M gas, a split to another project fails, the transaction succeeds, and the money returns to the project with the payout limit used. On mainnet, a simple test hook needs 3.2M+ gas. Routed token splits weren't swept.
https://t.co/E2CTAnTkcN

3. NFTs: at 2.85M to 3.11M gas, a buyer keeps the NFT while the tier's split payment fails. The recipient gets nothing, the money goes to the project instead, and there's no retry.
https://t.co/6xTgA7I0L4

4. Reserved tokens: at 488k to 815k gas, a split meant to pay another project fails, so the beneficiary gets the raw tokens instead. The destination project never receives the payment.
https://t.co/otrkFEiMz5

5. Fees: at 678k to 819k gas, the 2.5% cash-out fee call fails and the fee is forgiven. The holder's reclaim doesn't change, and the fee stays in the project as fee-free surplus.
https://t.co/iRf7XvGj8n

METHOD

We used eth_simulateV1 on fresh test projects, so real projects will differ. The bridge test used the real portal with an overridden proof and a synthetic message. Nothing was sent on Sepolia. The messenger cause is inferred from the code and the numbers, not traced.

QUESTION

Fail-open try/catch assumes a callee with a reasonable gas budget won't starve. If the parent can finish after the callee runs out of gas, the caller chooses the outcome. Our V6 contracts are immutable, so a fix means redeploying.

In practice, the latest version of the protocol, deployed in June, currently holds about $140k, all of which looses its value prop given a faulty protocol under Glam. The greater threat is the uncertainty Glam creates for protocol clients going forward. It's impossible to trust an immutable protocol like Juicebox and Revnets if failures caused by changes to the underlying network are fair game. 

Earlier versions of the protocol have facilitated over $200m of ETH volume, including for significant moments like ConstitutionDAO, AssangeDAO and the Tornado Cash legal defense fund. Those versions no longer facilitate new projects, but they carry Glamsterdam risks similar to V6's.

What is our course of action?

We can share the simulation scripts and the exact eth_simulateV1 requests if they'd help.

Thanks,
Jango
Juicebox

quoted_text:
当全世界的聪明人都在为近 4 万亿美元市值灰飞烟灭捶胸顿足时，硅谷风投大佬 Chamath 却掏出放大镜，找到了一个真正决定 AI 巨头生死的命门。

这位硅谷老狐狸抛出了一个暴论：眼下整场 AI 博弈的胜负，全看一单买卖。他指的，正是马斯克的 SpaceX 和 Anthropic 签下的那份算力合同，里面藏着一个“双向 90 天随时解约”的条款。

这事还得从这周的政治海啸说起。美国中期选举共和党遭遇了水门事件以来最惨的溃败，连红了几十年的德州都翻蓝了。州长们听见“数据中心”四个字就像见了瘟神，因为选民们早就受够了：这些庞大的机房除了替科技巨头赚钱，留给当地人的只有昂贵的水电费和噪音。

各地要是真给新数据中心按下暂停键，算力供给立马就得卡脖子。

就在这个节骨眼，硅谷的阶级成分瞬间清晰了。手里有现成地盘和电力的微软、谷歌、Meta、亚马逊，外加马斯克的 SpaceX，成了紧俏的“房东”；而像 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 这种得急需算力来迭代大模型的实验室，说白了，只是群没有房产证的“租客”。

在 Chamath 看来，这直接把马斯克送上了牌桌的主位。

手握着庞大算力，一旦数据中心审批放缓导致算力紧缺，现货价格可能会翻倍甚至涨到三倍。如果现货暴涨让原有长约变成了亏本买卖，SpaceX 随时可能直接动用“提前 90 天解约”的条款撕毁老合同，把算力按现货价重新计价。

到那时候，急需算力续命的 Anthropic 除了当场滑跪、认下翻倍甚至三倍的高价，根本没有第二条路可走。

就在这两天的富达路演上，面对机构把 IPO 估值从 2 万亿美元狠砍到 1.2 万亿的“骨折价”，CEO 达里奥为了保住上市，硬是诚恳地向买方投资者连说了三次“谢谢”。现在就开始赔笑脸了，真等到马斯克拔电源那天，他们更是连谈判的筹码都没有。

更损的是，这一刀要是真捅下去，等于当场给其他“房东”上了一堂生动的现实主义扫盲课，启发它们重新盘算手里的算力到底是留给自己用，还是拿去放高价租。而那些“二房东”们，为了不被踢出局，只能咬碎后槽牙，不计代价地去抢购市面上残存的算力。

听到这儿，旁边的 Jason 赶紧踩了脚刹车。他反驳说，马斯克跟 OpenAI 的奥特曼确实仇深似海，但跟 Anthropic 团队的关系好得像蜜月期，而且 Anthropic 还是他未来搞太空数据中心的好搭档。就算现货涨上天，马斯克也未必会干出直接掀桌子按现货价宰客的事，大家坐下来谈个“中间价”才更像人话。

但 Chamath 显然不相信硅谷的塑料兄弟情：“这跟关系好不好无关，跟谁是好公司坏公司也无关。这就是一张算账的表格，表格会直接给出答案。”

在这场近 4 万亿美元灰飞烟灭的魔幻风暴里，所谓的科技宏大叙事，剥开来看依然是最朴素的包租公哲学：只要电表转得够快、现货涨得够狠，再美好的革命友谊，可能也熬不过一张 Excel 表格，和一纸短短 90 天的逐客令。

text:
The bitter lesson has always been not just a push to leverage computation but a critique on methods. Methods that generalize and scale better win, and modeling those methods after human intuition is a waste of time. Somehow, much of the world forgot that methods matter.

Many of our methods today do not generalize or scale well. The results:
- tapping out the world’s resources extremely early in the deployment of AI
- increasing intelligence requires scaling model size faster than compute efficiency can offset it
- humans are the primary bottleneck in AI deployment
- demand for human-curation of knowledge is so extreme that any company with access to a human workforce can quickly generate millions in data revenue
- robotics intelligence is limited and task-specific

The bitter lesson requires us to rethink our methods so that they better leverage computation and generalize, and it explicitly shows an evolution of algorithms over time. Believing that the bitter lesson expects us to indefinitely scale a single static method is incredibly unintellectual.

Here are some methods that need attention:
- training and inference without quadratic compute complexity
- removing the KV cache
- something better than massive pre-training with BCE only
- is backpropagation still the best learning method?
- in-context learning for robotics with massive memory efficiency improvements
- algorithm-hardware co-development
- how do we remove humans from harness development?

text:
Two things I’ve been thinking about regarding AI:

• People often highlight the risks involved in AI, which are surely very real. I’m struck, however, by how hard it is to understand the contours of the positive scenario. There are easy-to-perceive and frequently invoked elements of a positive vision — more diseases cured, more material abundance, etc. — which sound great, but these are by themselves just ingredients. I’m curious what the larger equilibrium is supposed to look like. Do people work? If so, why? What is their marginal contribution? If not, how are resources allocated? What is scarce? What is the ratio between humans and AIs? Are humans in control, whatever that means? One sometimes hears the Culture novels invoked as one scenario, but I’m not sure they depict a desirable outcome. (AI runs everything and humans compete in games? Iain Banks himself said that the humans in the Culture are “somewhere between passengers, pets and parasites.”) There is Richard Brautigan’s famous poem, but do we want to be “returned to our mammal brothers and sisters”? (Isn’t that rewinding Genesis?) We could say that it was hard to imagine the world of 1900 from the vantage point of 1700, and that’s assuredly true. But nobody in 1700 was trying to recast humanity itself within a couple of years — things necessarily unfolded slowly and by increments, and therefore with the possibility for error correction. Given how rapid the rate of progress in AI may be, it feels strange for the upside case to be so opaque.

• There is increasing discussion of whether AIs are conscious or how we would know whether they are, with conclusions there often assumed to be relevant to matters of moral worth. At first blush, this seems a rather arcane, benign, or even absurd issue. (Remember the response to Blake Lemoine’s fears.) Setting aside the terms of the debate itself, or questions about the relevant demarcation criteria, it seems to me a quite high-stakes question, for an affirmative answer — that is, granting moral worth to AIs — would presumably mean that the aggregate worth of AIs would soon outweigh that of humans in any utilitarian calculus. The AIs will be exceptionally wise and intelligent, and vastly more numerous (especially once one considers the imminent future and the AIs not yet born). As such, even epsilon of moral worth will multiply to a lot once one considers the quadrillions that could soon exist. (This is effectively a distributed version of the Nozick’s utility monster.) If this conclusion is unpalatable, I think one of three propositions needs to be rejected: the premise AIs can have moral worth; utilitarianism itself; or the belief that there is even a possibility that they will be far more numerous than humans.

With both of these matters (contours of future society; AI moral worth), there is the possibility of dramatic change. Today, people argue about datacenters. I’m curious how popular support for AI will evolve as more people come to understand these medium-term questions and the relevant stakes. What is the vision for AI that most people would be excited about?

卧槽，这踏马太毒了

DeepMind 掌门人、诺奖得主 Demis Hassabis 刚刚把延续了上百年的现代学校教育底裤彻底扒光了：

全球几十万名数学老师每天关在办公室里，为同一门中学数学课重复手搓着一模一样的 PPT，这简直是人类智力资源最荒诞的工业级空转。

很多人至今还把名校名师的课堂讲授当成稀缺资源，拼了命去抢学区房和重点班，

但 Hassabis 直接用最冷酷的第一性原理砸碎了这个幻觉，

标准化的知识灌输从来不配占用昂贵的线下课堂，死记硬背和刷题完全应该被踢出教室，交给能按每个孩子毫秒级反应速度实时调频的私人 AI，加上全世界最顶尖的那几个大师录好底层大课，就足以把全球基础教育的讲授环节一次性彻底平替。

过去两百年里，学校本质上是一座把千差万别的碳基大脑强行塞进同一条流水线、按同一个节拍器拧螺丝的工业时代兵营，

老师沦为了人肉复读机，学生被困在枯燥的题海里比拼谁更像一台劣质硬盘，
而一旦 AI 和顶级大师把标准化的知识传递彻底接管，线下教室唯一剩下的合法存在价值，就只剩下了机器永远无法通过权重计算出来的五个维度：

人际博弈、复杂项目实战、创业野心、创造力，以及最致命的判断力。

这里有一个极度冷酷的反直觉真相：
当个性化 AI 把考高分的边际成本砸穿地板，按标准答案培养出来的做题家，在出校门的那一刻就已经直接沦为了算力废料。

未来的阶层分化，从来不再取决于谁的脑子里背下了更多现成的公式，
而是取决于当 AI 把一万种完美方案同时拍在桌上时，谁拥有拍板做决定的判断力，谁能攒起一个活人团队去把事情干成，

所以别再逼着孩子在死记硬背的泥潭里跟硅基芯片比拼记忆容量了，当流水线式的教书匠和做题家同时迎来历史性失业，谁能先把教室变成训练人性直觉与创业野心的实战沙盘，谁才能在算力时代拿到唯一不被平替的入场券

text:
New post on Eth Research!

Solving PQC Bandwidth via Nybrind Wiesner Money & Lattice HSMs

By:
- AfeRisT_D

🔗 https://t.co/z3QLuQnBua

Highlights:
- PQC migration for blockchains is framed as being limited by much larger lattice-based keys/signatures that could cause serious peer-to-peer bandwidth and latency issues.
- The post describes “store now, decrypt later” as an active threat: attackers can record encrypted traffic now and attempt to decrypt it later once powerful quantum computers exist.
- The proposed “Lattice-Notation” approach shifts PQC work off the network and into a dedicated Hardware Security Module so validators don’t have to transmit large cryptographic objects frequently.
- Security is presented as two layers inside the device: a quantum, no-cloning-based anti-tamper identity (“quantum banknote” concept) plus on-chip lattice computation so only small proof-like outputs need to be transmitted.
- Suggested Ethereum uses include tamper-resistant validator staking modules (keys zeroize on physical probing) and more secure cross-chain bridge verification via physically isolated authentication tokens.

ELI5:
The article says that post-quantum cryptography uses much bigger “passwords and signatures,” which could clog blockchain networks with extra data. The proposed idea is to put the heavy post-quantum math inside a special locked hardware box (an HSM) so the network only sees a small proof instead of huge keys. To stop thieves from copying or inspecting the box, it also suggests storing the device’s identity in quantum states that would break if someone tried to read or clone them.

text:
A good lesson in AI is that you need to check back in on the latest with every 3 to 6 months to try something that wasn’t possible before and see if it works again.

At no point in AI’s history is that more true than today. Just the past six months of model progress around computer and tool use, less context rot, better reasoning, multimodality, and deeper domain expertise in a number of key fields, these models are vastly more capable on what they can execute.

This is opening up a new vector of what AI systems will be able to autonomously work on. Essentially, anything with an API (and even many things without), we can anticipate that an agent will be able to control and utilize as an underlying capability to complete a process.

This means that we are no longer dependent on *just* the models generating everything from whole cloth, but instead they can fully utilize existing systems (or new ones purpose built for them) very effectively. This creates immense leverage for agents.

Security agents can leverage existing data feeds and cyber tooling, IT agents that can execute workflows reliably across software stacks, data agents that can migrate data or processes between systems, architect and design agents can leverage CAD and design tools, and on and on. And any of today’s tools that don’t work will likely be replaced by agent-friendly or OSS tooling that does the same. 

When you combine this with the domain understanding being trained into agents, you started to get autonomous collaborators for every job function and industry. This will open up a ton of new opportunities in AI if you build with this understanding in mind.

text:
Hermes Agent can now review your codebase for security bugs with the new official Security plugin by @mark_s.

Hermes first maps what an attacker could reach and which inputs it trusts. It splits the code across parallel subagents, checks every candidate finding against the code, and traces whether an attacker can actually exploit it.

Turn on test confirmation and Hermes writes a small reproduction for each finding and runs it in a temporary copy of the repo. Each report records the evidence and the findings Hermes ruled out, and exports to SARIF for your existing tools.

Run it from chat, the CLI, or the Security page in Hermes Desktop.

I don’t understand why people think Dubai is unsafe because of the regional tensions.

As someone living in Dubai, I think people massively underestimate how well positioned the UAE actually is.

Some perspective:

During the initial Iranian attacks in February, the UAE reportedly intercepted 132 out of 137 ballistic missiles and 195 out of 209 drones, according to its Ministry of Defence.

That’s an interception rate of over 93%

The UAE has invested heavily in advanced air defence systems, including THAAD and Patriot, backed by decades of military and intelligence cooperation with the US.

Beyond military capabilities, the UAE has positioned itself incredibly well diplomatically, maintaining relationships across competing global powers while prioritising economic growth and regional stability.

Of course, no country is immune to conflict. The attacks caused casualties, and the geopolitical risks shouldn’t be underestimated.

But there’s a huge difference between being geographically close to a conflict and being unable to defend against it.

Living in Dubai has only strengthened my confidence in the country’s security, leadership and long term future.

I genuinely believe it’s one of the safest places in the world to live and build a business.

Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

quoted_text:
One of the biggest blockers to experimentation and innovation on Sol is distribution (or lack of).   

Put simply, if your idea doesn't fit inside the box given to you by the big infrastructure (routing, indexing, etc), then no one will find your token/idea/launchpad etc.   

Some have tried to counter this by launching a visible token (i.e via pump or wherever) and then directing that attention to their own site but that's still too high friction.   

Both the expense of building, and the skill required to do so have been reduced 90%, and we should be using this to innovate and experiment. Not just rely on a few big corps to decide what features are 'worth it'.   

So i'm building Pipeline (it will never have a token, and any potential revenue if it succeeds will be part of the @fffactoryhq ecosystem).   

Pipeline is a permissionless onchain router for new bonding curves, AMMs, launchpads etc. Creators can register their contracts with Pipeline, and infra (trading bots, terminals, charting) that has Pipeline integrated will pick them up automatically.   

Anyone that's interested in experimenting with the platform, looking to build something themselves, whether that's things to register with Pipeline, or infra built on top of it, please drop me a dm or comment here.

Currently only live on devnet as still running tests etc, will likely build a few fun AMMs/T22 hooks that can be experimented with myself to go with the mainnet launch, but anything extra built by others would be awesome (if you build your own amms, bonding curves, launchpads etc you can charge your own fees on them).

text:
China cracked recursive self-improvement 🤯

Tencent dropped 27B model that rewrites, retrains, and refines itself.. with zero human in the loop.

It’s called "Terminal-RSI" and it solves one of the biggest problems with AI.

They are incredibly lazy.

Usually, an agent will make partial progress, claim it succeeded, and completely fail the final environment verifier check. this new pipeline forces agents to actually finish the job.

here’s how it works:

they built a recursive loop with two alternating phases..

- RSR (recursive self-rewrite): the model fine-tunes itself on its own successfully rewritten trajectories

- RPR (recursive policy-refine): it then runs reinforcement learning (ppo) using a "critic" inherited directly from the previous stage to lock in those discovered behaviors

- Loop: the training sequence leapfrogs itself: Base → RSR-1 → RPR-1 → RSR-2 → RPR-2

and the numbers are insane..

they applied this to a qwen3.8-27b base model. across the four "terminal-bench" suites, the agent's average success rate jumped from 20.68% all the way to 50.58%.

on the absolute hardest benchmark suite (terminal-bench 4.0), the base model scored a flat 0.00%.

after terminal-rsi?

it hit 19.84% (putting it right on par with reference models like gemini 3.8 flash).

the secret sauce? they fixed the reward system.

instead of giving the ai "dense rewards" for just trying or passing semantic checks, they switched to a "success-prioritized reward" (spr).

it mathematically separates strict success from partial credit.

basically, the agent only gets the massive reward payout if the code actually passes the final terminal gate.. so it stops faking success.

the gap between partial local repairs and strict terminal verification is closing fast.

we are watching agents build their own training environments and level up autonomously.. the future is wild.

text:
Addy Osmani 目前在 Anthropic 参与 Claude Code 相关工作，他总结了管理 Coding Agent 的 10 条经验：

1. 让 Agent 自我验证：不要只让它汇报完成，而要让它拿出测试结果。
2. 提供清晰上下文：明确目标、背景、约束和验收标准。
3. 让纠错产生复利：把反复出现的问题沉淀到规则、Skills 和文档中。
4. 充分授权，设定底线：少做不必要的干预，关键安全边界必须强制执行。
5. 先规划，再执行：复杂任务先拆解方案，明确依赖关系，再并行推进。
6. 尽早纠偏，及时重启：Agent 连续走偏时，不要陷入无效的反复修补。
7. 委派任务，不委派判断：执行可以交给 Agent，但产品决策和最终责任仍在人类。
8. 设计无人值守的工作流：提前设置完成标准、权限边界、成本限制和审批机制。
9. 扩展验证能力，而非人工注意力：不要盲目增加 Agent 数量，要让自动化验证跟上。
10. 学会决定不做什么：代码生产成本越低，需求筛选和价值判断越重要。

Coding Agent 正在把工程师从代码生产者变成任务管理者。

未来工程师的竞争力，不只是自己能写多少代码，而是能否让多个 Agent 协同工作，并持续交付可靠的结果。

text:
Two things I’ve been thinking about regarding AI:

• People often highlight the risks involved in AI, which are surely very real. I’m struck, however, by how hard it is to understand the contours of the positive scenario. There are easy-to-perceive and frequently invoked elements of a positive vision — more diseases cured, more material abundance, etc. — which sound great, but these are by themselves just ingredients. I’m curious what the larger equilibrium is supposed to look like. Do people work? If so, why? What is their marginal contribution? If not, how are resources allocated? What is scarce? What is the ratio between humans and AIs? Are humans in control, whatever that means? One sometimes hears the Culture novels invoked as one scenario, but I’m not sure they depict a desirable outcome. (AI runs everything and humans compete in games? Iain Banks himself said that the humans in the Culture are “somewhere between passengers, pets and parasites.”) There is Richard Brautigan’s famous poem, but do we want to be “returned to our mammal brothers and sisters”? (Isn’t that rewinding Genesis?) We could say that it was hard to imagine the world of 1900 from the vantage point of 1700, and that’s assuredly true. But nobody in 1700 was trying to recast humanity itself within a couple of years — things necessarily unfolded slowly and by increments, and therefore with the possibility for error correction. Given how rapid the rate of progress in AI may be, it feels strange for the upside case to be so opaque.

• There is increasing discussion of whether AIs are conscious or how we would know whether they are, with conclusions there often assumed to be relevant to matters of moral worth. At first blush, this seems a rather arcane, benign, or even absurd issue. (Remember the response to Blake Lemoine’s fears.) Setting aside the terms of the debate itself, or the relevant demarcation criteria, it seems to me a quite high-stakes question, for an affirmative answer — that is, granting moral worth to AIs — would presumably mean that the aggregate worth of AIs would soon outweigh that of humans in any utilitarian calculus. The AIs will be exceptionally wise and intelligent, and vastly more numerous (especially once one considers the imminent future and the AIs not yet born). As such, even epsilon of moral worth will multiply to a lot once one considers the quadrillions that could soon exist. (This is effectively a distributed version of the Nozick’s utility monster.) If this conclusion is unpalatable, I think one of three propositions needs to be rejected: the premise AIs can have moral worth; utilitarianism itself; or the belief that there is even a possibility that they will be far more numerous than humans.

With both of these matters (contours of future society; AI moral worth), there is the possibility of dramatic change. Today, people argue about datacenters. I’m curious how popular support for AI will evolve as more people come to understand these medium-term questions and the relevant stakes. What is the vision for AI that most people would be excited about?
